name: Eratosthenes' Measurement of the Earth
aliases: Eratosthenes' measurement of the Earth's circumference
Eratosthenes and the size of the Earth
statement: From the different noon shadows in two cities, Eratosthenes estimated the circumference of the whole Earth with geometry.
statementAccent: estimated the circumference of the whole Earth with geometry
meaning: Eratosthenes' measurement of the Earth is the ancient determination of the Earth's circumference made by Eratosthenes of Cyrene, the Greek scholar who directed the great Library of Alexandria, around 240 BC. Using only geometry and observations of the Sun's shadows, he produced the first known reasonably accurate estimate of the size of the planet. He knew that at noon on the summer solstice the Sun stood directly overhead at Syene, modern Aswan, so that a vertical object cast no shadow and the Sun reportedly lit the bottom of a deep well. At the same time in Alexandria, to the north, a vertical rod, a gnomon, cast a shadow showing that the Sun was about seven degrees from overhead, roughly one-fiftieth of a full circle. Reasoning that the difference in the Sun's angle equalled the angle between the two cities as seen from the Earth's centre, and taking the distance between them as about five thousand stadia, he multiplied to get a circumference of about two hundred fifty thousand stadia, later given as two hundred fifty-two thousand. Depending on the exact length of the stadion he used, this was strikingly close to the true circumference. The measurement is a celebrated early triumph of quantitative science.
mechanism: Eratosthenes' method rests on simple geometry and two reasonable assumptions: that the Earth is a sphere and that the Sun is so far away its rays arrive essentially parallel. At noon on the summer solstice the Sun was directly overhead at Syene, casting no shadow, while at the same moment at Alexandria, on roughly the same meridian to the north, a vertical gnomon cast a shadow indicating the Sun was about seven point two degrees away from the vertical. Because the Sun's rays are parallel, this angle of the shadow at Alexandria equals the angle subtended at the centre of the Earth by the arc between Alexandria and Syene. Since seven point two degrees is one-fiftieth of a full three hundred sixty degrees, the distance between the two cities must be one-fiftieth of the whole circumference. Taking that distance as about five thousand stadia, he multiplied by fifty to obtain a circumference of about two hundred fifty thousand stadia, a figure sometimes refined to two hundred fifty-two thousand, which corresponds to a round seven hundred stadia per degree. The accuracy of the result therefore depends on the length of the stadion, an ancient unit whose value is not known with certainty, so how close his answer was to the modern forty thousand kilometres cannot be stated exactly.

examples.text: At noon on the summer solstice the Sun stood overhead at Syene, casting no shadow and reportedly lighting the bottom of a well.
At the same moment a vertical rod at Alexandria cast a shadow showing the Sun about seven degrees from overhead, one-fiftieth of a circle.
Taking the cities as five thousand stadia apart and that as one-fiftieth of the whole, he found a circumference near two hundred fifty thousand stadia.

whyItMatters: Eratosthenes' measurement of the Earth is a celebrated milestone in the history of science, the first known attempt to determine the size of the planet by reasoning and measurement rather than guesswork, and an early triumph of the geometric and quantitative approach to nature. Working around 240 BC with nothing but shadows, a gnomon, and the geometry of a sphere lit by a distant Sun, Eratosthenes arrived at a circumference that, on plausible readings of his units, was remarkably close to the modern value, an astonishing achievement for the ancient world. The measurement demonstrates the power of a good idea and careful reasoning to reach far beyond direct experience, deducing the dimensions of the whole Earth from observations in just two cities. It also shows the scientific method in embryo: clear assumptions, a measurable quantity, and a logical inference from data to conclusion. Retold ever since as a model of ingenuity, it remains a favourite illustration of how much can be learned from simple observations combined with mathematics.

limits: Eratosthenes' measurement is rightly celebrated, but its precise accuracy cannot be stated with confidence because the length of the stadion he used is genuinely uncertain, with historians' estimates ranging widely; on a shorter stadion his result is within a few percent of the true circumference, while on a longer one it is off by well over ten percent, so claims that he was accurate to within a percent should be hedged. Several details come from later or traditional accounts rather than his own surviving writings, including the vivid image of the Sun lighting a well at Syene and the conventional date of about 240 BC, so these are best given with words like reportedly and around. His input distances and angles were themselves approximate, and Syene is not exactly on the Tropic nor precisely on Alexandria's meridian.
misreadings: Eratosthenes' measurement is not known to have been accurate to within a percent; because the length of his stadion is uncertain, how close he came to the true value cannot be pinned down and should be hedged. The well at Syene and the exact date are drawn from later tradition, not his own surviving words, so they are reported rather than certain. And he did not measure the Earth directly but inferred it from shadows in two cities using geometry, so treating his accuracy as precisely known, the traditional details as documented fact, or the method as a direct measurement, misreads a brilliant but approximate ancient estimate.
origin: The determination of the Earth's circumference by Eratosthenes of Cyrene, director of the Library of Alexandria, around 240 BC, from the difference in noon solstice shadows at Alexandria and Syene; the first known reasoned estimate of the planet's size.
